moduleTitle: Being gurmukh rather than manmukh, and the elimination of haumai

note.specFocus: Spec 3.1.7.1 Key beliefs: the importance of being gurmukh (God-centred) rather than manmukh (man-centred) and the elimination of pride or ego (haumai).
note.summary:
GURMUKH AND MANMUKH
• Gurmukh – literally 'facing the Guru'. A gurmukh is God-centred: they live by the Guru's teaching, constantly remember God's Name (simran), accept God's will (hukam) and develop virtues such as humility, contentment and compassion. They see God's light in all people and serve them. The gurmukh is the ideal Sikh and is moving towards mukti.
• Manmukh – literally 'facing one's own mind'. A manmukh is self-centred: they follow their own desires, are ruled by haumai and the five thieves (lust, anger, greed, attachment, pride), are attached to maya and forget God. They may be religious outwardly, but their heart is not turned to God. They remain in the cycle of rebirth and are restless and unsatisfied.
The Guru Granth Sahib contrasts the two repeatedly, for example in Guru Nanak's Siddh Gosht (Ang 938–946), where he explains to yogis that it is by becoming gurmukh, not by leaving society, that God is found.

HAUMAI (ego, self-centredness)
• Haumai means 'I, I' – the sense of self as separate from God and from others, putting 'me' first.
• It is the root barrier to mukti; the five thieves grow from it.
• 'Haumai is a chronic disease, but it also contains its own cure' (Guru Angad, Asa di Var, Ang 466). The cure is turning the self towards God.

HOW HAUMAI IS ELIMINATED
1. Nam japna / simran – meditating on 'Waheguru' and the Mool Mantra.
2. Following gurbani – reading or hearing the Guru Granth Sahib, taking a daily hukamnama.
3. Sewa – humble service, e.g. washing dishes, cleaning shoes, cooking langar.
4. Sangat – the support of the community.
5. Humility in worship – covering the head, bowing, sitting on the floor.
6. God's grace (nadar) – ultimately haumai is removed by God's gift.
7. Amrit Sanskar – the initiate symbolically gives up their old self and caste identity.

WHY IT MATTERS
Being gurmukh is the path to jivan mukti and union with God; it also transforms relationships – a gurmukh treats others equally and lives honestly (kirat karna) and generously (vand chhakna).

DIVERSITY
Some Sikhs stress the inner, meditative side of being gurmukh; others the outward Khalsa discipline (five Ks, rehat). Some argue haumai can be completely eliminated (as in the Gurus); others that it is a lifelong struggle. Humanists value self-esteem and may see some 'ego' as healthy.

CONTEMPORARY EXAMPLE
Volunteers at the langar in British gurdwaras – including professionals such as doctors and lawyers – wash pots and serve food alongside others, deliberately setting aside status to reduce haumai.

KEY TERMS: gurmukh, manmukh, haumai, simran, hukam, hukamnama, nadar, sewa, sangat.

questions.question:
Which one of the following terms describes a person who is God-centred?
A Manmukh
B Gurmukh
C Haumai
D Sahajdhari
questions.modelAnswer: B – Gurmukh. Gurmukh means 'facing the Guru' – a person whose life is centred on God and the Guru's teaching. Manmukh is the opposite (self-centred), haumai is ego, and sahajdhari is a Sikh who has not taken amrit.
questions.examTip: Read all four options before choosing. Only one is correct; write the letter clearly. If unsure, cross out options you know are wrong first.

questions.question:
What does the Sikh term 'haumai' mean?
A Grace
B Ego or self-centred pride
C Honest work
D The community of Sikhs
questions.modelAnswer: B – Ego or self-centred pride. Haumai literally means 'I, I' or 'I-am-ness' – seeing oneself as separate from God and at the centre of everything. Grace is nadar, honest work is kirat karna and the community is the sangat/Panth.
questions.examTip: Read all four options before choosing. Only one is correct; write the letter clearly. If unsure, cross out options you know are wrong first.

questions.question: Give one characteristic of a manmukh.
questions.modelAnswer: Any one of: self-centred; driven by ego (haumai); controlled by the five thieves (lust, anger, greed, attachment, pride); forgets God's Name; attached to maya/worldly things; follows their own mind rather than the Guru.
questions.examTip: A 1-mark short response needs one accurate, relevant point only. A short phrase or sentence is enough; do not waste time explaining.

questions.question: Give one way Sikhs believe haumai can be overcome.
questions.modelAnswer: Any one of: nam japna (meditation on God's Name); sewa (selfless service); following the Guru's teaching/gurbani; joining the sangat; God's grace; developing humility.
questions.examTip: A 1-mark short response needs one accurate, relevant point only. A short phrase or sentence is enough; do not waste time explaining.

questions.question: Explain two ways in which the aim of becoming gurmukh influences Sikhs today.
questions.modelAnswer:
First way: Sikhs try to follow the Guru Granth Sahib rather than their own desires. Many take a hukamnama (a random reading from the Guru Granth Sahib) each day and try to apply its teaching, so their decisions are guided by the Guru not by ego.

Second way: Sikhs do sewa to put others first. For example, a Sikh might volunteer to cook langar or help at a food bank, because a gurmukh serves others selflessly rather than seeking praise or reward.
questions.examTip: Give two separate ways. For each, make a simple point (1 mark) and then develop it with an example, consequence or detail (2 marks). Two undeveloped points score only 2.

questions.question: Explain two ways in which belief about haumai influences the way Sikhs behave.
questions.modelAnswer:
First way: Sikhs practise humility in worship. They cover their heads, remove shoes, bow before the Guru Granth Sahib and sit on the floor, showing that they are not more important than anyone else and helping to reduce ego.

Second way: Sikhs try to avoid boasting about good deeds. Because doing sewa or giving money in order to be praised would feed haumai, many Sikhs give dasvandh or serve in the langar quietly, seeing it as God's work rather than their own achievement.
questions.examTip: Give two separate ways. For each, make a simple point (1 mark) and then develop it with an example, consequence or detail (2 marks). Two undeveloped points score only 2.

questions.question:
Explain two Sikh teachings about the difference between gurmukh and manmukh.
Refer to sacred writings or another source of Sikh belief and teaching in your answer.
questions.modelAnswer:
First teaching: A gurmukh is God-centred – they face the Guru, remember God's Name and accept God's will (hukam). Because they live by the Guru's teaching, they develop virtues such as humility, contentment and compassion, and move towards mukti.

Second teaching: A manmukh is self-centred – they follow their own mind, are ruled by haumai and the five thieves and are attached to maya. As a result they remain trapped in the cycle of rebirth and feel restless and unhappy, even if they are wealthy.

Source: Guru Nanak's Siddh Gosht and many other hymns in the Guru Granth Sahib contrast the two. For example, gurbani teaches that the gurmukh is absorbed in the Name and so is at peace, while the manmukh wanders in doubt. Applying this, Sikhs see every choice as a step either towards God (gurmukh) or away (manmukh).
questions.examTip: Explain two teachings, each developed (2 + 2 marks), then name a source of Sikh authority AND apply it to the question (2 marks). Naming the Guru Granth Sahib with an Ang number, or a Guru's teaching, and showing how it supports your point is the safest way to get the source marks.

questions.question:
Explain two Sikh teachings about haumai.
Refer to sacred writings or another source of Sikh belief and teaching in your answer.
questions.modelAnswer:
First teaching: Haumai is the main barrier between a person and God. It makes people see themselves as separate from God and from others, and it is the root of the five thieves – lust, anger, greed, attachment and pride. As long as haumai rules, the soul stays in the cycle of rebirth.

Second teaching: Haumai can be cured. It is overcome by meditating on God's Name, listening to the Guru, doing sewa and through God's grace. When haumai is removed, a person becomes gurmukh and recognises God's light in everyone.

Source: In Asa di Var, Guru Angad writes 'Haumai is a chronic disease, but it also contains its own cure' (Ang 466). This shows both teachings: haumai is a serious illness, but by turning the self towards God through grace, the same self can be healed.
evidence: 'Haumai deeragh rog hai, daaroo bhee is maahi' – Ang 466

Naming the Guru Granth Sahib with an Ang number, or a Guru's teaching, and showing how it supports your point is the safest way to get the source marks.

questions.question:
“It is impossible to completely overcome haumai.”
Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
• refer to Sikh teaching
• give reasoned arguments to support this statement
• give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
• reach a justified conclusion.
questions.modelAnswer:
ARGUMENTS IN SUPPORT

Haumai is described as a 'chronic disease' (Ang 466) – a long-lasting illness built deep into human nature. Every person has a sense of self and self-interest, so getting rid of it completely may seem unrealistic.

Even good actions can feed haumai. A person who does sewa might become proud of being humble, or proud of their religious knowledge. This shows how subtle ego is, and why many people struggle with it all their lives.

The five thieves that grow from haumai are constantly encouraged by modern society – advertising feeds greed and attachment, social media encourages pride and comparison. From a non-religious point of view, a healthy ego is necessary for self-respect and survival, so eliminating it entirely would not even be desirable.

ARGUMENTS FOR A DIFFERENT VIEW

The same verse says haumai 'also contains its own cure' (Ang 466). Sikh teaching insists that through nam japna and the Guru's grace, haumai can be overcome. If it could not, mukti would be impossible, and the whole Sikh path would be pointless.

Sikhs believe the Gurus were completely free from haumai, and the Guru Granth Sahib describes the gurmukh and the jivan mukt as people who live without ego while still in the world. So it has been achieved, and it is the goal for every Sikh.

Sikhism also gives practical tools: sewa, sangat, humility in the gurdwara, the Amrit Sanskar where the initiate surrenders their old identity, and daily prayer. These are designed to reduce ego step by step. The five khands show this as a journey ending in grace (Karam Khand) and union (Sach Khand).

CONCLUSION

Completely overcoming haumai is extremely difficult, and most Sikhs would admit they are still struggling. However, Sikh teaching clearly says it is possible through God's grace, as the example of the Gurus shows. So the statement is too strong: haumai cannot be overcome by human effort alone, but with grace it can be completely overcome.
evidence: 'Haumai deeragh rog hai, daaroo bhee is maahi' – Ang 466

questions.question:
“You can be a good person without being gurmukh.”
Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
• refer to Sikh teaching
• give reasoned arguments to support this statement
• give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
• reach a justified conclusion.
questions.modelAnswer:
ARGUMENTS IN SUPPORT

Many people who do not believe in God are kind, honest and generous. Humanists argue that morality is based on reason, empathy and the effects of actions on others, not on religious belief. A non-religious volunteer at a homeless shelter is clearly a good person.

Sikhism itself teaches that God's light is in everyone (Ang 13), so it is consistent to say that good people exist in all religions and none. The Guru Granth Sahib includes writings of Hindu and Muslim saints, showing that goodness is not limited to Sikhs.

Guru Nanak praised the honest carpenter Bhai Lalo over the corrupt rich man Malik Bhago because of how they lived, not what label they carried. So goodness is shown in actions.

ARGUMENTS FOR A DIFFERENT VIEW

For Sikhs, being gurmukh means being God-centred, and they would say true goodness comes from this. A person who does good deeds while forgetting God may still be acting from haumai – wanting praise or feeling superior. Only when ego is overcome by remembering God is goodness fully pure.

Sikhs believe virtues are ultimately gifts of God's grace. 'Truth is higher than everything, but higher still is truthful living' (Ang 62) refers to living in line with God's truth. Without this, a person may be outwardly good but remain manmukh, trapped in the cycle of rebirth.

Also, being gurmukh is not about being Sikh by name; it is about facing God. A non-Sikh who lives selflessly and humbly may already be close to gurmukh in Sikh eyes, which shows the two ideas are closely linked.

CONCLUSION

In everyday terms, people can certainly be good without being gurmukh, and Sikh teaching recognises goodness in all. But from a Sikh perspective, goodness reaches its full meaning only when it flows from a God-centred life free from ego. So the statement is true at a human level, but Sikhs would say being gurmukh is what makes goodness complete and leads to mukti.
